topics.original_record:
{
    id: 'sound-signals',
    division: D,
    subject: 'Sound and sampling',
    title: 'Sound as a signal, and how it is sampled',
    level: 'entry',
    status: 'established',
    summary:
      'Sound is a small, fast variation of air pressure over time. A computer stores it as samples taken at a fixed rate. The sampling theorem says exactly when those samples lose nothing: when the signal contains no frequency at or above half the sample rate.',
    definitions: [
      { term: 'signal', text: 'A function x: ℝ → ℝ (continuous time) or x: ℤ → ℝ (discrete time), here pressure deviation against time.', status: 'established' },
      { term: 'sampling theorem', text: 'A signal with no frequency content at or above B is determined by samples taken at rate f_s > 2B (Whittaker–Nyquist–Shannon).', status: 'established' },
      { term: 'aliasing', text: 'A component at frequency f > f_s/2 produces the same samples as one at |f − k f_s| for some integer k: the sampling map has a kernel, and those frequencies collide.', status: 'established' },
    ],
    constraints: ['Sampling is linear; aliasing is its kernel acting on frequency: sinusoids that differ by multiples of f_s become identical samples.'],
    examples: [
      { title: '44.1 kHz', body: 'At f_s = 44 100 Hz, a 30 000 Hz tone aliases to |30 000 − 44 100| = 14 100 Hz.' },
    ],
    prerequisites: [],
    transformations: ['sampling', 'quantization', 'resampling'],
    visualLesson: 'The interval ring’s tones are generated by your browser at its audio sample rate, only after you choose to hear them.',
    challenge: { prompt: 'At f_s = 8000 Hz, which frequency does a 5000 Hz tone alias to?', hint: '|f − f_s|.', answer: '3000 Hz.' },
    sources: [SHANNON49, OPPENHEIM],
    sourceStatus: 'paper',
    domainAdapter: 'interval-ring',
    glossary: ['signal', 'kernel', 'sampling'],
  },
topics.subject: Sound and sampling
topics.title: Sound as a signal, and how it is sampled

topics.original_record:
{
    id: 'pitch-frequency',
    division: D,
    subject: 'Pitch',
    title: 'Pitch, frequency and the logarithm',
    level: 'entry',

      'Equal steps of pitch are equal ratios of frequency. That is why musicians count in semitones and cents, which are logarithms: twelve semitones make an octave, a doubling of frequency.',
    definitions: [
      { term: 'frequency of a MIDI note', text: 'f(m) = 440 · 2^{(m − 69)/12} Hz, with A4 = MIDI 69 = 440 Hz by convention.', status: 'established' },
      { term: 'cent', text: 'One hundredth of an equal-tempered semitone: the interval with ratio r measures 1200 log₂ r cents.', status: 'established' },
      { term: 'pitch class', text: 'A pitch modulo octaves: an element of ℤ/12 in twelve-tone equal temperament.', status: 'established' },
    ],
    constraints: ['Pitch is perceptual; frequency is physical. For complex tones the perceived pitch can correspond to a missing fundamental.'],
    examples: [
      { title: 'Middle C', body: 'C4 is MIDI 60: f = 440 · 2^{−9/12} ≈ 261.63 Hz.', compute: 'music:frequency:60' },
    ],
    prerequisites: ['sound-signals'],
    transformations: ['transposition (add semitones)', 'octave equivalence (mod 12)'],
    visualLesson: 'Pitch classes sit around the ring like hours on a clock.',
    challenge: { prompt: 'How many cents is a perfect fifth of ratio 3/2?', hint: '1200 log₂ 1.5.', answer: 'About 701.96 cents, 1.96 cents wider than the equal-tempered fifth.' },
    sources: [SETHARES, FLETCHER_ROSSING],
    sourceStatus: 'textbook',
    domainAdapter: 'interval-ring',
    glossary: ['pitch', 'interval', 'frequency'],
  },
topics.subject: Pitch
topics.title: Pitch, frequency and the logarithm

    division: D,
    subject: 'Interval geometry',
    title: 'Interval geometry: walking the circle of twelve',
    level: 'entry',
    status: 'established',
    summary:

    definitions: [
      { term: 'interval class', text: 'An element k of ℤ/12; transposition by k is x ↦ x + k mod 12.', status: 'established' },
      { term: 'orbit length', text: 'The cyclic subgroup ⟨k⟩ ⊆ ℤ/12 has 12 / gcd(12, k) elements.', status: 'established' },
      { term: 'circle of fifths', text: 'The orbit of 0 under +7: 0 7 2 9 4 11 6 1 8 3 10 5. It visits every pitch class because gcd(7, 12) = 1.', status: 'established' },
    ],
    constraints: ['This is the geometry of twelve-tone equal temperament. Just intonation does not close: twelve pure fifths overshoot seven octaves by the Pythagorean comma (≈ 23.46 cents).'],
    examples: [
      { title: 'Augmented triad', body: 'Stepping by 4 from C: C, E, A♭, C. Three classes: the augmented triad, an equilateral triangle on the ring.', compute: 'music:orbit:4' },
    ],
    prerequisites: ['pitch-frequency'],
    transformations: ['transposition', 'inversion (x ↦ −x)'],
    visualLesson: 'Choose an interval and the atrium relights: the number of lit arches equals the orbit length, and their hue walks the colour wheel by 30° per semitone.',
    challenge: { prompt: 'How many pitch classes does stepping by 3 (minor third) visit?', hint: 'gcd(3, 12).', answer: '12 / 3 = 4: the diminished seventh chord.' },
    sources: [TYMOCZKO, LEWIN],
    sourceStatus: 'textbook',
    domainAdapter: 'interval-ring',
    glossary: ['interval', 'orbit', 'pitch'],
  },

    title: 'Spectra: the discrete Fourier transform',
    level: 'intermediate',

      { term: 'DFT', text: 'X[k] = Σ_{n=0}^{N−1} x[n] e^{−2πikn/N}, k = 0, …, N − 1. It is an invertible linear map ℂᴺ → ℂᴺ.', status: 'established' },
      { term: 'spectrum', text: 'The magnitudes |X[k]| (and phases arg X[k]) as a function of frequency bin k.', status: 'established' },
    ],
    constraints: ['The DFT assumes the N samples are one period of a periodic signal; a tone not fitting the window leaks into neighbouring bins.'],
    examples: [
      { title: 'A pure bin', body: 'x[n] = cos(2π·3n/8) for N = 8 has X[3] = X[5] = 4 and every other bin 0.' },
    ],
    prerequisites: ['sound-signals'],
    transformations: ['DFT', 'inverse DFT', 'windowing'],
    visualLesson: 'In the acoustic realm, a stained-glass window shows a spectrum: each pane is a frequency bin.',
    challenge: { prompt: 'Is the DFT injective?', hint: 'It is invertible.', answer: 'Yes: its kernel is {0}. Spectral processing loses information only through what is done to the spectrum afterwards.' },
    sources: [SMITH_DFT, OPPENHEIM],
    sourceStatus: 'textbook',
    domainAdapter: null,
    glossary: ['spectrum', 'kernel', 'phase'],
  },

topics.original_record:
{
    id: 'time-frequency',
    division: D,
    subject: 'Time–frequency representations',
    title: 'Time–frequency: the spectrogram and its limit',
    level: 'advanced',
    status: 'established',
    summary:
      'A spectrogram slices a signal into short windows and takes the spectrum of each. Short windows give sharp timing and blurred pitch; long windows the reverse. Gabor (1946) showed the trade-off is a mathematical limit, not an engineering one.',

      { term: 'short-time Fourier transform', text: 'STFT{x}(m, k) = Σ_n x[n] w[n − mH] e^{−2πikn/N} for a window w and hop H.', status: 'established' },
      { term: 'Gabor limit', text: 'For a signal’s time spread σ_t and frequency spread σ_f, σ_t σ_f ≥ 1/(4π); equality holds for Gaussian windows.', status: 'established' },
    ],
    constraints: ['No window can be arbitrarily short in time and narrow in frequency at once.'],
    examples: [
      { title: 'Two notes close together', body: 'Two tones 10 Hz apart need a window of roughly 100 ms or more to be separated in frequency; within that window, their onsets blur together.' },
    ],
    prerequisites: ['fourier'],
    transformations: ['windowing', 'hop size change'],
    visualLesson: 'A long corridor of frames: each frame is a window, each pane in it a frequency.',
    challenge: { prompt: 'Halving the window length does what to frequency resolution?', hint: 'Bins are f_s/N apart.', answer: 'It doubles the bin spacing, so frequency resolution halves.' },
    sources: [GABOR, SMITH_DFT],
    sourceStatus: 'paper',
    domainAdapter: null,
    glossary: ['spectrum', 'window'],
  },

    definitions: [
      { term: 'labelled transition system', text: 'A triple (S, Σ, →) of a set of states S, an alphabet of labels Σ, and a transition relation → ⊆ S × Σ × S. We write s —a→ t when (s, a, t) ∈ →.', status: 'established' },
      { term: 'deterministic', text: 'A transition system is deterministic when, for every state s and label a, there is at most one t with s —a→ t. Then each label acts as a partial function on states.', status: 'established' },
      { term: 'run', text: 'A run on a word a₁…aₙ is a sequence of states s₀, s₁, …, sₙ with sᵢ₋₁ —aᵢ→ sᵢ for every i.', status: 'established' },
    ],
    constraints: ['A run exists only if every step is a transition; a missing transition is a failure of the structure, not of the word.', 'Non-determinism means a word can have several runs; the system then denotes a relation, not a function.'],
    examples: [
      { title: 'A door with a lock', body: 'States {locked, closed, open}; labels {unlock, open, close, lock}. The word unlock·open is a run from locked to open; the word open from locked has no run.' },
      { title: 'A counter', body: 'States ℕ; one label inc with n —inc→ n+1. It is deterministic and total: every word incᵏ has exactly one run from each start.' },
    ],
    prerequisites: [],
    transformations: ['restriction to reachable states', 'determinization (subset construction)', 'product of two systems'],
    visualLesson: 'In the atrium, the six doors are states and the bridges are transitions. Walking a word lights the run, step by step.',
    challenge: { prompt: 'In the door system, which states are reachable from closed using only the labels open and close?', hint: 'Try each label from closed, then from the states you reach.', answer: '{closed, open}. Locked is never reached without the label lock.' },
    sources: [SIPSER, HMU],
    sourceStatus: 'textbook',

    glossary: ['transition', 'state', 'word', 'run'],

      { term: 'syntactic admissibility', text: 'A word w ∈ Σ* is syntactically admissible iff w ∈ ℒ. This does not depend on the structure.', status: 'house' },
      { term: 'semantic realizability', text: 'w is realizable at x iff ⟦w⟧(x) ≠ ∅, where ⟦w⟧ is the relational composition of its moves.', status: 'house' },
      { term: 'labelled transition system (as used by CGT)', text: 'The pair (𝔄, ⟦·⟧) is an ordinary labelled transition system; CGT adds the admissibility language and a cost model.', status: 'established' },
    ],
    constraints: ['A word can be admissible but unrealizable (the grammar allows it, the structure lacks the step), or realizable but inadmissible (the structure allows it, the grammar forbids it).', 'CGT is a working research manuscript, not peer reviewed; results marked “proved here” are self-checked.'],
    examples: [
      { title: 'Binary tree navigation', body: 'Σ = {L, R, U}. In a complete tree of height 2, the word LL is realizable from the root but LLL is not. If ℒ forbids “U immediately after L” (no back-tracking), then LU is inadmissible before the tree is even consulted, although the step exists.' },
      { title: 'The Bridge Grammar', body: 'Words are walks across the atrium. “FRPG” is realizable if each consecutive pair of doors has a bridge, and admissible if its bridge types avoid two golds in a row.' },
    ],
    prerequisites: ['transition-systems', 'finite-automata'],
    transformations: ['intersection with ℒ (product construction)', 'change of representation', 'compilation of words to single operations'],
    visualLesson: 'Two lamps hang over each walk: a gold lamp for admissibility and an ivory lamp for realizability. They are separate lamps on purpose.',
    challenge: { prompt: 'Give a word that is realizable but not admissible in the initial Bridge Grammar.', hint: 'The gold bridges are R–P and A–W. Find a walk that crosses gold twice in a row.', answer: 'None exists in the initial layout, because no two gold bridges share a door.
